problem: Single-LLM VLN agents couple perception, planning, and control in one model, causing cognitive overload, hallucination, and decision drift on long-horizon multi-target instructions. Existing multi-agent frameworks use parallel negotiation with high overhead and are not designed for embodied navigation.
motivation: Real-world long instructions with several landmarks expose error accumulation in monolithic agents. Distributed cognition suggests splitting functions among specialized agents that verify each other, which could reduce the load on any single model and improve robustness.
key_idea: A master agent orchestrates four specialist sub-agents (observation, task planning/verification, control execution with mapping, memory) in a Plan-Perceive-Act-Evaluate loop, plus local (per-step) and global (post-task) reflection that feeds an experience bank.
insight: Ablations show each role matters, especially the execution agent (removal gives SR 0) and the task planner (SR 5.2). Dynamic verification matters more than hierarchical decomposition (SR 15.6 vs 18.4 when removed). Removing memory or reflection costs about 8-10 SR points. Caveat: the evaluation is small and non-standard (50 self-generated instructions on a real robot, baselines re-implemented), and the LLM backbones differ from what the baselines used.
method: Master Agent: LLM state machine (PLANNING/PERCEPTION/ACTION/EVALUATION/REFLECTION) that selects the next sub-agent and passes context; does not perceive or act itself.
Task Planning Agent: LLM decomposes the instruction into a landmark-centric sub-task sequence, then verifies sub-task completion from observation and history (progress phi vs threshold tau).

Observation Agent: MLLM processes 4 directional views into obstacles with depth, landmarks with bearing, traversability, and scene context, then distills a task-oriented description (salience filtering, traversability, target localization, spatial relations).

Control Execution Agent: builds an incremental geometric coordinate map from odometry (4 candidate waypoints per step) and a topological adjacency graph; picks among MoveForward, Turn ±90°, Stop using shortest-path heuristics.

Memory Agent: stores full trajectory history and, post-hoc, structured experience tuples (scene features, erroneous action, cause, corrective action), retrieved by embedding similarity as risk alerts or planning hints.

Local reflection: each step the candidate action is checked against the observation and against high-risk memory cases (similarity > tau_risk); conflicting actions are vetoed and replaced, with rollback after collisions.
Global reflection: after each task, history is segmented into episodes, root causes of failures are inferred, and new experience tuples are written to memory.

setting.backbone: GPT-4-Turbo / GPT-5.2 Pro (frozen, cloud API); GPT-5.2 Pro as MLLM for the Observation Agent
setting.training_data: none (training-free, no scene-specific fine-tuning); experience bank accumulated online from ~50 tasks
setting.observation: egocentric RGB-D (ORBBEC DaBai, 640x480) from four cardinal directions plus odometry

numbers_note: No standard benchmarks (R2R etc.) are used; the split label 'test' is a placeholder for the paper's own real-world test set. Reflection metrics: EDR 18.7%, RA 85.2%, RSR 72.3%, MRA 78.4%.
results: On its own real-robot benchmark MA-CoNav reaches SR 25.6, OSR 37.6, SPL 15.62, NE 2.93 and KPA 69.89. The strongest baseline, the multi-agent RCTAMP, gets SR 8.4, and the single-agent NavGPT and MapGPT get SR 0. Its navigation length (33.56 steps) is higher than the single-agent baselines, which the authors attribute to frequent local reflections.
limitations: Evaluation only on a small self-built real-world set (50 LLM-generated instructions); no standard VLN benchmarks, and baselines were re-implemented, so comparisons are not directly comparable to published numbers.
Absolute SR is still low (25.6%) and paths are long; the system depends on cloud LLM APIs (latency, cost) and the LLM's weak spatial reasoning.
The experience bank is reused in only about 35% of new tasks; the coarse discrete action space (90° turns) is a further constraint.
